content: The WHO's interim guidance on the termination of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) emphasizes the importance of virus sharing among Member States. This sharing of Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) biological materials is critical for global monitoring, risk assessment, and the development of safe and effective influenza vaccines. The Standard Material Transfer Agreement 1 (SMTA1) outlines the rights and obligations of laboratories within the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) when transferring PIP biological materials both within GISRS and to external parties. This ensures a structured and transparent process for the exchange of these materials. Benefit-sharing mechanisms aim to make the advantages derived from the sharing of PIP biological materials more accessible to countries, prioritizing public health risks and needs. For example, Standard Material Transfer Agreement 2 (SMTA2) establishes binding contracts between WHO and recipients of PIP biological materials outside GISRS, such as vaccine manufacturers, biotechnology firms, and research institutions. These recipients are required to assess and commit to contributions to the PIP benefit-sharing system based on their capacity and nature of operations. An annual partnership contribution is mandated for influenza vaccine, diagnostic, and pharmaceutical manufacturers utilizing WHO GISRS. These funds are allocated to enhance global pandemic influenza preparedness and response. Additional benefits include laboratory and surveillance capacity building, regulatory capacity strengthening, and the establishment of antiviral and inter-pandemic vaccine stockpiles. The governance of the PIP Framework is supported by three pillars: oversight by the World Health Assembly, promotion of implementation by the WHO Director-General, and guidance and monitoring by an Advisory Group. WHO acts as the secretariat, collaborating with public and private partners to ensure efficient implementation of the framework. PIP biological materials include human clinical specimens, wild-type human H5N1 virus isolates, and other influenza viruses with pandemic potential. It also encompasses modified viruses developed by GISRS laboratories, such as candidate vaccine viruses created through reverse genetics or high-growth reassortment. Additionally, RNA extracted from these viruses and complementary DNA (cDNA) encoding viral genes are included. GISRS plays a vital role in monitoring circulating influenza viruses globally, identifying antigenic drift, and detecting new viruses with pandemic potential. It comprises WHO Collaborating Centres, National Influenza Centres, H5 Reference Laboratories, and Essential Regulatory Laboratories. GISRS also ensures the availability of virus isolates for vaccine updates and provides logistical support to public health laboratories for identifying non-seasonal influenza infections. Member States are responsible for timely sharing of influenza viruses with pandemic potential, contributing to the benefit-sharing system, and supporting GISRS. WHO issues biannual recommendations on seasonal influenza vaccine composition and reviews candidate vaccine viruses for pandemic subtypes like H5N1. During an emerging pandemic, WHO expedites the selection, development, and distribution of vaccine viruses and related reagents, relying on timely virus sharing through GISRS. Emergency risk management for health (ERMH) is a comprehensive approach to managing health risks from various hazards, including pandemics, chemical spills, and natural disasters. It integrates hazard-specific preparedness and response systems into a unified framework. ERMH aims to strengthen country and community capacities, ensure essential components are in place, and link these components across health systems, disaster management systems, and other societal mechanisms. ERMH emphasizes ethical considerations, ensuring that emergency measures limiting individual rights are necessary, reasonable, proportional, equitable, and compliant with national and international laws. It also advocates for a whole-of-society approach, recognizing the interdependence of public and private organizations in pandemic preparedness. Effective planning is essential to mitigate potential disruptions, such as social and economic instability, supply shortages, and reduced productivity. The six essential components of ERMH include policies and resource management, planning and coordination, information and knowledge management, health infrastructure and logistics, health and related services, and community emergency risk management capacities. These components are supported by appropriate policies, legislation, financing mechanisms, and human resource planning to ensure a robust response to health emergencies.
